en: Preface to the *Record of the Treasure Treasury of the Chan Gate*:
Now, as for our Elder Kāśyapa, he lit the lamp of Chan from the heart of Mahākāśyapa; the ocean of the teachings poured forth from the mouth of Ānanda.

Thus, it was settled that Chan and the Teachings were distinct paths from the outset. Yet, those who hold office within the Teachings, upon hearing of that which is "separate from the teachings," [regard it with suspicion].

As for the assertions of the *Chuan* (The Transmission), it describes one with a "blue face and white eyes," asking, "What kind of evil words are these? Alas! How can the magnification of "self" and "other" reach such an extreme?

Therefore, I am filled with indignation and summon my courage; disregarding my own limitations—like measuring the ocean with a ladle or peering through a tube—I shall examine this through the lens of the Three Gates.
What are these Three Gates? They are Chan and Teaching, which have become muddled and confused. Thus, in the upper fascicle, I establish the distinction between Chan and Teaching.
The Gate of Discernment: Those who slander are the various lecturers; therefore, the middle fascicle establishes the Gate of the Various Lecturers’ Submission.
The Gate of Circulation: This concerns rulers and ministers; therefore, the lower fascicle establishes the Gate of Rulers and Ministers’ Veneration and Faith.

These three gates cited here are all ancient, weighty words; they are not mere speculative assertions. If they are not speculative assertions, there may well be those among people who believe them. Thus it is said.
Thus it is called the Treasure Trove of the Chan Gate. Preface by the Sramana Naewon-dang Jinjeong Daecheonsa Tianyi Mengdan from海东 (Haidong).
Written on the [blank] day of the eleventh month in the thirtieth year of the Zhiyuan era, the Gui-si year.

*Chánmén Bǎozàng Lù* (Record of the Jewel Treasury of the Chan Gate), Volume Upper.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Tiāndí of Hǎidōng.
The Section on Distinguishing Between Chan and Teaching (Twenty-five Cases).
When Vairocana Buddha first attained perfect enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree, he transmitted mind-to-mind and did not establish written words.
He caused the great assembly to realize and awaken all at once; only the Elder Kāśyapa entered the secret and inconceivable ground.
The ocean-like assembly of eighty thousand bodhisattvas, including Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, did not recognize the place where Kāśyapa had entered. (From the *Jātaka-sūtra*)

When the Brahma King arrived at the assembly on Vulture Peak Mountain, he offered a golden *pāra* flower to the Buddha and offered his own body as a seat, requesting the Buddha to preach the Dharma for the sake of all living beings.
When the World-Honored One ascended the seat, he held up a flower to show the assembly;
among the hundreds of billions of beings in the realms of humans and devas, none could fathom it, yet only Kāśyapa broke into a smile. The World-Honored One said, "I possess the True Dharma Eye."
The wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa* is concealed; it was entrusted to Mahākāśyapa. In the *Mahābrahmādeva-Questions-to-the-Buddha-Resolution-of-Doubts Sūtra*, it is said:
"Upon the sea, winds shift and various waves arise; because one contemplates conditions that transcend the world, the three thousand [worlds] are differentiated and expounded."
Because the depths of the ocean floor are extremely profound, it is a place where wind and shadows do not reach; such is the realm of the Tathāgata’s mind, serene and without boundaries.
The Chan master Zongdao of Lingnan commented: “The waves are a metaphor for the ocean of the Buddha’s teachings as they manifest according to the capacities and inclinations of sentient beings.”
The elucidation of the five thousand scriptures: "The bottom of the ocean" means, for example, that the bottom of the ocean is exceedingly deep;
it is not moved by the shifting of wind and shadows. The winds of the three kalpas cannot reach its depths. The profound intent of our Buddha is likewise thus:
the deepest of the deep, the most mysterious of the mysterious; it cannot be conceived by the mind and cannot be deliberated upon by words. *Prajñā-dhara-sāgara* (The Ocean of Prajñādhara).
The *Xuanji* (Profound Record) provides a shadowy indication of the fundamental tenet.
The Second Patriarch of the Tang land, the Great Master Huìkě, asked Bodhidharma: "I do not ask about the entrustment of the True Dharma for now;

I ask whom the Śākya Patriarch transmitted it to, and from where was it obtained? Please explain this out of your great compassion as a precedent for future generations. Bodhidharma said: "As for me..."
The Five Regions of India: A Tradition of the Patriarchs’ Teachings. Now, for your sake, I shall explain and reveal them. The verse says:
The True Refuge, the Patriarch, dwelt in the Snowy Mountains; In a hut among the thickets, he awaited Śākyamuni. In the year of Renwu, he received the transmission of the Patriarchal Seal;
His mind attained the Patriarchal School’s teaching simultaneously. *The Secret Record of Bodhidharma*
The Sixth Patriarch of the Tang land, the Great Being Huineng, was once visited by a monk from Youzhou who addressed him, saying:

"The Buddha taught the Dharma of the Three Vehicles, yet he also spoke of the Supreme Vehicle. Your disciple does not understand; I pray that you will grant me your compassion. The Patriarch told him:
"To see, hear, recite, and read is the Small Vehicle. To awaken to the Dharma and understand its meaning is the Middle Vehicle. To practice according to the Dharma is [the Great Vehicle]."
In the Mahāyāna, one recognizes one’s own fundamental mind and perceives one’s own original nature. All phenomena are fully understood and all practices are simultaneously perfected.
Without discarding anything, one remains free from all views and appearances; moment after moment, there is no dwelling. This is the Supreme Vehicle.
The *Pudeng Lu* (Record of the Universal Lamp) quotes Prajñātāra as saying: "Our Buddha descended from Tuṣita Heaven and entered the womb of Māyā directly for thirty [days]."
To the three men, he bestowed a collective prophetic record, saying: "I have the Dharma of the Mind; I entrust it all to you.

Each of you shall await your time and transmit it one to another, secretly guarding the fundamental tenet so that it does not perish. This is called the 'Separate Transmission Outside the Teachings. Accordingly, the verse says:
Within the womb of Māyā, the essence of the Dharma-realm is one suchness. The thirty-three patriarchs, simultaneously..."
The secret prophecy. Regarding the transmitters of the Dharma-treasury, they are not uniform;
there are three categories: first, the Exoteric Teachers, who [transmit] the sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras of the various vehicles;
second, the Esoteric Teachers, who [transmit] the Yoga initiation, the five families, the homa rites, and the methods of the three secrets and maṇḍalas; third, the Mind-Teaching Teachers.

"Directly pointing at the human mind to see one's nature and become a Buddha" is the Dharma of Chan. The next is the Wheel of the Exoteric Teachings (*vyākaraṇa-dharmacakra*), which takes Kāśyapa Mātanga as its founder.
The next is the Wheel of Ritual Commands (*ājñā-dharmacakra*), which is the Esoteric Teaching (*guhyamantra*) and takes Vajrabodhi as its founder.
He is the progenitor of the first transmission. Next is the Mind Wheel (Citta-cakra), for which Bodhidharma is the progenitor.

Therefore, those who transmit the Wheel of the Dharma (Dharma-cakra) transmit the sound of the Dharma through the sound of the Dharma; those who transmit the Wheel of the Teaching Command (Śāsana-cakra) transmit the secret through the secret;
and those who transmit the Mind Wheel transmit mind through mind. These three teachings, three wheels, and three patriarchs have come from the West.
In the East, [the Dharma] transformed the ordinary into the sagely and flowed through fifteen generations.
According to the *Sengshi lüe* (Brief History of the Sangha), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The Buddhas have severed attachment to dharmas;

they neither establish scriptures nor adorn their speech. Thus, what was the Great Sage’s intention? How could it ever have resided necessarily in the teachings? Furthermore, a sutra says: "The teaching of the Sūtras..."
It is like a finger pointing at the moon. Once one sees the moon and understands what was pointed out, that finger is ultimately not the moon itself.

How could this be intended to make people cling to the traces of the teaching? Furthermore, a sutra states: "From the Deer Park to the end at the Vārāṇasī River, within these two intervals, I have never spoken a single word.
This is precisely what is meant by the "separate transmission outside the teachings. — *Zhengzong ji* (Record of the True School)
At that time, Śākyamuni was not merely the master of meditative transformation.
It is said that the Buddha who is the master of the transformative practice of this school is neither Vairocana nor Śākyamuni, yet he can manifest as Vairocana and manifest as Śākyamuni.

He is neither the ten bodies nor the three bodies, yet he can manifest as the ten bodies and manifest as the three bodies. Therefore, he is called the King of the Dharma; this very one is the single essence of the three bodies.
This is not comparable. One naturally possesses the numinous light that illuminates past and present; why must one inscribe the *svastika* upon the breast? Regarding the *Bianzong ji*:
Now, the "separate transmission outside the teachings" is the common dharma of all Buddhas and patriarchs. This is because this dharma is not [expressed by] words.
It is that which words can attempt to approximate; hence it is called "beyond the teachings" (*kyōge*).

Because one awakens to the essence of the Buddha-mind without passing through stages or ranks, receiving the seal of the Dharma directly, it is called "special transmission" (*bekuden*). As for the teachings, they proceed from having words to being without words.
As for the mind, it proceeds from being without words to being beyond words. From being without words, it reaches the state of no-...
As for its name, no one is able to define it; therefore, it is given the provisional name "dhyāna.

People of the world do not understand its origin, and some claim that it can be known through study, attained through reflection, or perfected through practice, calling it *dhyāna*. This is translated as "calm contemplation" (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*).

Calm contemplation refers to clarifying the spirit while sitting upright, ceasing external conditions, and binding the mind; it is merely one method that assists in the accomplishment of contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā*).

For what reason did the World-Honored One, at the time of his imminent parinirvāṇa, secretly transmit [the Dharma] to Kāśyapa, so that it was passed down through thirty-three generations in succession without interruption?
Therefore, that which is transmitted by the Dharma does not consist of borrowing the teachings to practice meditation;
rather, it is the path of directly pointing to the human mind to see one’s nature and become a Buddha. *Zumen Kanjōroku* (Record of the Rectification of the Patriarchal Gate)
The Fifth Patriarch of the Tang land, the Great Master Hongren, summoned the Sixth Patriarch, the Great Master Huineng, and addressed him, saying:
"The appearance of all Buddhas in the world is for the sake of one great matter. According to the capacities of beings—whether small or large—they are guided accordingly;

thus there have arisen the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), the three vehicles (*triyāna*), and the doctrines of sudden and gradual, which serve as the gateways of teaching. Nevertheless, [the ultimate truth] is the unsurpassed, subtle, secret, perfect, and luminous [Dharmakāya]."
The true Eye of the Right Dharma was entrusted to the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, the foremost disciple.
It was transmitted in succession through twenty-eight generations until it reached Bodhidharma. Upon arriving in this land, he met the Great Master Huineng, who inherited it and passed it down to me.
I now entrust to you this Dharma-treasure and the robe I have transmitted. Guard it well yourself; do not allow it to be severed.

In the *Chuan Deng Lu*, the Buddhas are said to speak of the bow and the patriarchs speak of the string. To speak of the string is to point to the sublime path of the direct transmission of the Chan gate—a path that does not rely on words.

[The text] explains: it directly reveals the fundamental essence of the mind-body (*citta-tattva*), like the string of a bow. As for the various teaching-gates (*śāsana-mukha*), the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) is the direct path, while the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*) are the circuitous paths;
thus, it is better to directly present the fundamental essence of the mind-body and demonstrate it within the activity of the mind. Why is this?
That which is taught in the One Vehicle teachings is the perfectly interfused *dharmadhātu* of the non-obstruction of phenomena (*shishi wuai*). This non-obstruction...
Only when obstructive phenomena are resolved within the Dharma-realm does one return to the single-flavor Dharma-realm;
only by wiping away the traces of this single-flavor Dharma-realm does the "One Mind" revealed by the Patriarchs manifest. Thus, one knows that the various teachings are not direct.
In Chan Master Shunde’s Record, the ten Buddha altars and the single Sea-Seal (Haiyin) encompass the three worlds in their entirety; the inexhaustible ocean of nature is unified as one.
"Flavor. The single flavor of subsiding marks is my Chan.

When the Venerable Zhenjing Wen composed this verse regarding the Dharma Master Shizhi Wenzzi, he saw that Chan practitioners were rejecting Buddhism and truly considered it to be non-canonical; he was so moved that his hair stood on end.
He lamented only that Chan practitioners reject Buddhism, failing to see that Chan practitioners cleanse the sun of the Buddha. I find this difficult to accept.
This teaching has clear textual authority: it is said that this is neither the Śrāvaka vehicle, nor the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, nor the Bodhisattva vehicle, nor even the Buddha vehicle.
It is the most supreme of the supreme meditations (dhyāna) transmitted from our ancestors. [The questioner] asks: By what words should this be described?
To describe this Dharma-gate, he replied: When a monk asked Zhaozhou about the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West, he said, “The cypress tree in the courtyard.
This single phrase is something that has never before existed within the Dragon Palace or the Ocean Treasury. Venerable Jiyin recorded a monk asking:
"When did the Dharma of separate transmission begin? He replied: "At the time of the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he was concerned for the future."
Sentient beings merely rely on the literal words of the sutras and fail to understand the Buddha’s intent; they are like a poor man who counts another’s treasures, gaining no benefit whatsoever.
For this reason, the World-Honored One opened his blue-lotus eyes, looked toward Kāśyapa, and secretly entrusted [the Dharma] to him before the assembly.
—Recorded by Chan Master Yanshou.
Daomeng asked Yang Xuanzhi: "One who clarifies the mind-source of the Buddha without the slightest error, whose practice and understanding are in accord, is called a Patriarch.
Why, then, does he manifest the traces of a Śrāvaka? How can he transmit the mind that lies outside the teachings? He replied:
"To guide those of the Hīnayāna disposition, he provisionally assumes the appearance of a Śrāvaka. On the day of the separate transmission outside the teachings, he is no longer a Śrāvaka."
...this wisdom. The *Caneilin Jiping* (Collected Evaluations of the Chan Forest) states:
"Tang Shenqing did not favor those of the Chan school; he thus composed a book to suppress them, saying:

'As for their transmission of the Dharma, it was occasionally by Śrāvakas such as Kāśyapa and others. Although they had turned their minds [toward the Mahāyāna], they still possessed only small wisdom. How could they transmit [the Dharma]?"
The Buddha’s mind is sealed [in truth]. How stubborn is this Qing! You merely indulge your own likes and dislikes, failing to recognize the Great Sage.
Even if a transmitter of the Dharma manifests in the form of a śrāvaka, how could he be fully defined as a śrāvaka?
Is he not rather an arhat manifested by an emanation-body Buddha? As for those manifested by the Buddha, it is fitting that they possess the four dhyānas and the three samādhis.
Immeasurable merit is no different from that of the Tathāgata. Since it is no different from the Tathāgata, one transmits the Buddha’s seal of mind;

who would say this is not so? The *Zhengzong ji* states that true nature is neither defiled nor pure, and there is no distinction between ordinary beings and sages. However, as for Chan, there are levels of shallow and deep, with differences in stages and gradations.

"Distinctive" refers to the following: that which is practiced by those who harbor heterodox views while rejoicing in higher realms and loathing lower ones is the meditation of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika-dhyāna*).

That which is practiced by those who correctly believe in cause and effect, likewise through rejoicing and loathing, is the meditation of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-dhyāna*). That which is practiced by those who have realized the principle of the partial truth of self-emptiness (*ātma-śūnyatā*) is the meditation of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna-dhyāna*).

That which is practiced by those who have realized the true reality manifested through the emptiness of both self and phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*) is the meditation of the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna-dhyāna*).

As for Chan: if one suddenly awakens to the fact that one’s own mind is originally pure, fundamentally free from afflictions, and inherently endowed with the nature of untainted wisdom—realizing that this mind is itself the Buddha and ultimately not different from it—and practices in reliance upon this, this is the Chan of the Supreme Vehicle.
It is also called the Tathāgata’s Pure Dhyāna. That which has been transmitted from master to disciple within the lineage of the Dharma is this very dhyāna.
Furthermore, it is said that "transmitting mind by means of mind" was the statement of the Great Master Bodhidharma.
Because Master Ke subsequently asked, "What written texts or scriptures are there for the study and practice of this Dharma? the Great Master replied, "My Dharma is transmitted by means of the mind."
The Mind does not rely on written words; it is said that one follows the teacher’s instruction rather than taking literary phrases as the Way.

One must transcend the means of expression to grasp the meaning; grasping the meaning is precisely the transmission of the Mind. In the Chan gate, the state of being free from thought and non-thought is likewise the wiping away of traces and the blocking of errors within this context.
It is simply the transmission of mind by mind, a place of secret intent and reception that is not to be discussed here in terms of written records. — Guishan.
Preface to the *Fengcanyuan zhuiji* (Collection of Explanations on the Source of Chan) and the Original Record:
Someone asked Master Dazhu, "I, your disciple, do not yet know which is the most excellent among the Vinaya Masters, the Dharma Masters, and the Chan Masters.
The Master said, "Now, as for the Vinaya Master, he is one who upholds the Dharma-treasury of the *śīla-vinaya*, transmits the legacy of the long-lived [Arhats], and penetrates..."
Through upholding and transgressing the precepts, one masters what is permitted and what is prohibited; by maintaining dignified deportment, one practices the rules of conduct.

Reciting the three rounds of the *karmavācanā*, one establishes the primary cause for the four fruits of the path. Now, as for the Dharma Master: seated upon the lion throne, he pours forth the eloquence of a cascading river.
Facing a vast assembly, he unlocks the profound gate and opens the wondrous door of Prajñā, bestowing gifts equally with the three wheels of action rendered empty. As for the Chan Master:

Grasping its essential pivot, one directly realizes the source of the mind. Emerging and withdrawing, expanding and contracting, responding to things with total spontaneity, one brings events and principles into perfect equilibrium and suddenly beholds the Tathāgata.
One uproots the deep-seated roots of birth and death and attains the samādhi of direct presence. If one does not settle in dhyāna and meditative contemplation, [this will not be achieved].
Upon reaching this point, one must necessarily be left in total bewilderment. That person bowed in gratitude and withdrew.

This is from the *Record of Zen Master Dazhu Huihai*, concerning those companions who mistakenly grasp the true regulations and those who erroneously transmit the succession of the Patriarchs; some speak of the gates of the Sudden and the Gradual.
He regards this as the orthodox lineage. Furthermore, he takes up the teaching of the Perfect and Sudden (yuantun) to serve as the vehicle of the school (zongsheng).

Although the self-substance of the ocean of nature (xinghai) is ineffable and its phenomenal aspects are eternally quiescent, one cultivates the causes of the dharma-realm (faxie) in order to realize the fruit of the dharma-realm; hence it is said:

Within the realm of cause and effect, if one were to cite the wondrous intent of the esoteric transmission of the Patriarchal School, there is fundamentally no cause of the Dharma-realm, nor is there any fruit of the Dharma-realm;

there is neither wisdom-realization nor the distinction between the primary and secondary [the Buddha and his environment]. Because there is fundamentally no cause, there is no path for cultivating the myriad practices;
because there is fundamentally no fruit, there is no gate for realizing that fruit. Question: If it is discussed in terms of the Sea-Seal Samādhi, is this itself realization?

The essence is free from cause and free from effect. How can this be reconciled with the Mind-Seal of the orthodox tradition of the Chan school? Answer: It is similar yet not similar. What does this mean?
That which is called the "Ocean Seal" (Sāgaramudrā) is the point where cause and effect are compressed; it is the state where one returns to the extinction of cause and effect.

There is a trace of the beginning of cause, and a trace of the end of effect. If one speaks of that very moment, although there is neither cause nor effect, when tracing back to the origin, [it is otherwise].
There is cause and there is effect. If we speak in terms of the principle of Chan, there is fundamentally no cause for the Dharma-realm, nor is there any further extinction of that cause;

there is fundamentally no effect as the Dharma-realm, nor is there any further extinction of that effect. How could one, after extinguishing cause and effect, return to a state where neither cause nor effect exists?
Therefore, the ancient masters said: "The place where the Chan patriarchs transmit the mind is like a bird flying through the sky. [Question: Regarding suddenness...
In the Teachings, all dharmas are free from the marks of mental objects and free from the subject and object of recollection.
Each and every dharma is pure and unmixed, consisting solely of the merit of suchness; therefore, there is no one who can enter them, yet they are also pure liberation.

Why is this different from the Chan gate? Answer: The realm of the Buddhas is fundamentally free from thought. It is because thoughts arise that there are sentient beings. The multitude [of beings]...
If, for even a single thought-moment, no-thought arises, one is identical to all Buddhas; thus, the first stage is itself the Buddha-stage.

The three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sainthood are like the tracks of birds in the sky. As for the True Suchness that is realized, it is beyond words and beyond forms, utterly extinguished and without dependence.
Without thoroughly clarifying this prior understanding, there is no means to encompass and accomplish this practice. This practice is the practice of forgetting all artifice. However...
Thus, there is the *tathatā* that is realized; there is the essence of the wisdom that realizes it; there are the non-arising delusive thoughts; and there are the arising right mindfulness.

Although it is quiescent and devoid of sequential stages, there is a progression from the stage of faith (*śraddhā*) up to the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*). The Buddha-ground is itself the stage of faith.

If one discusses the Gate of Meditation (*chanmen*), fundamentally there is not a single thought. What thought could fail to arise? Since thought is fundamentally non-existent, [so too is] the stage of faith.

Why is it established? It is not established at the stage of faith. How could it exist at the stage of Buddhahood? Since its characteristics are not perceived through recollection, what characteristic is there to be separated from?

Since names are fundamentally non-existent, what names are there to be separated from? Therefore, it is not the same as the Sudden Teaching (*dun-jiao*). Regarding the two meanings of "forgetting emotions to accord with principle":

first, as for acceding to principle by relying on the teaching, it is like a Mahāyāna bodhisattva who, when the Buddha preaches the Hīnayāna, does not become stuck in the Hīnayāna, even though he preaches the Great [Vehicle].

Riding upon the [five] vehicles, one does not stagnate in the Mahāyāna. In explaining principle and phenomena, one does not stagnate in principle and phenomena. In explaining emptiness and form, one does not stagnate in emptiness and form.

In explaining the ultimate and the conventional, one does not stagnate in the ultimate and the conventional. Regarding each and every word and phrase of the dharmas of the five vehicles, one does not destroy provisional names;
they are perfectly fused and harmoniously integrated. Second, as for those who rely on dhyāna to accord with principle: the Buddha taught that the Mahāyāna is fundamentally without "great."

Regarding the vehicles: the Buddha spoke of the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), yet fundamentally there is no Small Vehicle. The Buddha spoke of principle and phenomena (*li-shi*), yet fundamentally there is no principle or phenomenon.

This extends even to the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*); all dharmas within the three realms are like a bird flying through the sky, leaving no trace whatsoever.

As the *Huayan shu* (Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra) states: "Above the Perfect and Sudden [teachings], there is a distinct school; this is the school that discards linguistic expression to realize the ultimate meaning. Someone may ask:

"What is the elucidation? What is the convergence? He replied: "There is no elucidation beyond the five teachings; it is the convergence of the principles of the five teachings—this is the Chan school.
In the *Chan-chapter Beyond the Teachings* by Master Xuangjue, it is asked:
"The *Chan-jing* (Dhyāna-sūtra) is a sūtra of the Hīnayāna; it should not be included among the path of the Patriarchal Gate. The *Laṅkāvatāra* is the [sūtra of] nature..."

Regarding the Dharma of our school, there is also a tradition which claims that this was brought by Dharmatrāta as proof for the *Cittamātra-dharmaparyāya* (Mind-Ground Dharma Gate), and that it was entrusted [to him] at the time of his death.
The answer is: this too is not possible. This sutra is a sutra of singular parables;
the reason Mount Laṅkā is established as a metaphor is that its peaks are steep and lofty, serving to represent how the great ocean of birth and death separates all sentient beings.
This is because it is intended for ordinary beings as well as those of the Two Vehicles. The text states: "Those who have not attained the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) cannot ascend this mountain;
it is only with the great sages (*mahāprajña*) and other such Bodhisattvas that the meaning of Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) is discussed.

The intention is to stimulate those of the Two Vehicles, causing them to abandon the Lesser Vehicle and aspire to the Great. Since its capacity is not yet fully developed, it can only be situated within the Vaipulya section. Furthermore, An[shigao]...

"Can this serve as evidence for the Patriarchal Gate (Zumen)? Question: Since the Patriarchal Gate takes neither the *Candragarbha-sūtra* nor the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* as its primary tenet, would it now be appropriate to establish the *Prajñāpāramitā* as its tenet?
Answer: This too is not permissible. Why? Because in the midst of the *Nirvāṇa-saṃnipāta*, my predecessor, the Father [the Buddha], spoke only thus:
'I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye (*saddharmakṣayanidhi*), which I entrust to Mahākāśyapa. He did not say..."
I have the Mahāprajñāpāramitā, which I entrust to Mahākāśyapa. In Sanskrit, *prajñā* is translated here as "wisdom" (*zhìhuì*).
If it is wisdom, then Śāriputra serves as its presiding lord. All teachings expounded prior to [the realization of] *prajñā* are merely frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*).
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "One should sweep away the dung of frivolous proliferation regarding all phenomena. One should know that this is *prajñā*.
This [teaching] is merely a great medicine for the śrāvakas to chew away their tumors and break up their masses; how could it be called the patriarchal master of the Chan school?
As for the *Chan jing*, the *Laṅkāvatāra*, and the *Prajñāpāramitā*, perhaps their teachings and principles are not yet fully perfected and do not suffice to accommodate all capacities;
thus, they differ from the Patriarchal Gate. In the *Avataṃsaka*, every atom and every world-realm manifests the pure and wondrous body of Vairocana.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* reveals the perfect clarity of the wondrous nature to all sentient beings; the *Lotus Sūtra* is the subtle and profound One Vehicle, encompassing and completing everything.
How is it that within the school of the Patriarchs there is yet a "separate transmission"? Answer:
When our Śākyamuni taught the Dharma, he regarded all sentient beings with a mind of equal compassion. Seeing them adrift or flowing in the ocean of birth and death, he [responded] accordingly...
According to the depth of the water, they ferry across and enter the sea. There, they spread out nets and meshes; they may encircle with rings or set up barriers, using poles or hooks.
For fish that are large—such as the *āo* (tortoise) or the *jīng* (whale)—they cast them into the great nets.
For those such as the *fáng* (bream) or the *zǔn* (trout), they throw them into the medium-sized nets. As for crabs, clams, oysters, and snails, they then use small nets to scoop and gather them.
They exhaustively emerge from the ocean of afflictions and ascend the mountain of Nirvana, ferrying across all sentient beings.
Among them was one creature whose scales were like vermilion fire, its claws like iron hooks, its eyes shooting rays of sunlight, and its mouth exhaling smoke.
Suddenly emerging from its lair, it beheld these various nets, traps, and snares set out to capture it; it then stretched its body and raised its claws.
In a brief moment, white waves were seen surging to the heavens and black winds obscuring the sun; just at midday, it suddenly became dark as night.
